{{Short description|Formula in general relativity}}
In [[general relativity]], the '''quadrupole formula''' describes the [[gravitational wave]]s that are emitted from a system of masses in terms of the (mass) [[quadrupole moment]]. The formula reads:

<math display="block"> \bar{h}_{ij}(t,r) = \frac{2 G}{c^4 r} \ddot{I}_{ij} (t-r/c), </math>

where <math> \bar{h}_{ij}</math> is the spatial part of the trace reversed perturbation of the metric, i.e. the gravitational wave.  <math> G </math> is the gravitational constant, <math> c </math> the speed of light in vacuum, and <math>I_{ij}</math> is the mass quadrupole moment.<ref>{{cite book |last=Carroll |first=Sean M. |author-link=Sean M. Carroll |title=Spacetime and Geometry: An Introduction to General Relativity |title-link=Spacetime and Geometry |publisher=Addison-Wesley |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-805-38732-2 |pages=300–307}}</ref>

It is useful to express the gravitational wave strain in the transverse traceless gauge, by replacing the mass quadrupole moment <math>I_{ij}</math> with the transverse traceless projection <math>I_{ij}^{TT}</math>, which is defined as:
<math display="block">{I}_{ij}^{TT} = \int \rho(\mathbf{r}) \left[r_i r_j - r_n \left(r_i n_j + r_j n_i\right) + \tfrac{1}{2} r_n^2 \left(n_i n_j + \delta_{ij} \right) + \tfrac{1}{2} r^2 \left(n_i n_j - \delta_{ij} \right) \right]  d^3 r</math>
where <math>\mathbf{n}</math> is a unit vector in the direction of the observer, <math>r_n \equiv \mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}</math>, and <math>r^2 \equiv \mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{r}</math>.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Creighton |first1=Teviet |title=Formulae and Details |url=http://www.tapir.caltech.edu/~teviet/Waves/gwave_details.html}}</ref>

The total energy carried away by gravitational waves can be expressed as:
<math display="block">\frac{d E}{dt} = \sum_{ij} \frac{G}{5 c^5} \left( \frac{d^3 I_{ij}^{T}}{dt^3} \right)^2</math>
where <math>I_{ij}^{T}</math> is the traceless mass quadrupole moment, which is given by:
<math display="block"> {I}_{ij}^T = \int \rho(\mathbf{x}) \left[r_i r_j - \tfrac{1}{3} r^2 \delta_{ij}\right]  d^3 r. </math>

The formula was first obtained by [[Albert Einstein]] in 1918. After a long history of debate on its physical correctness, observations of energy loss due to gravitational radiation in the [[Hulse–Taylor binary]] discovered in 1974 confirmed the result, with agreement up to 0.2 percent (by 2005).<ref>{{cite book | title = Gravity: Newtonian, Post-Newtonian, Relativistic | first1 = Eric | last1 = Poisson | first2 = Clifford M. | last2 = Will | publisher = [[Cambridge University Press]] | isbn = 9781107032866 | pages = 550–563 | date = 2014-05-29 }}</ref>
